beats.narration_text: Everyone knows the number — 128K, a million, whatever it is this month. Almost nobody knows what the number is counting, or what it costs, or why the middle of it is where things go to be forgotten. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'counting what, exactly…'
output lines resolve, already answered

props.segment: What a Context Window Really Is
props.command: Models advertise a context window in tokens. What is actually being measured, what does holding it open cost the hardware, and does a bigger number really mean the model remembers more?
output: tokens, not words — about 75% of the count
the KV cache is the real bill, paid in VRAM
open is not the same as recalled

beats.narration_text: Every time you talk to an LLM, it reads everything — your prompt, the conversation history, its own previous answers — all at once, from a fixed-size buffer. That buffer is the context window. Think of it as a conveyor belt: whatever fits on the belt, the model sees. Whatever falls off the end is gone.

show.event: the belt draws across the frame under a glowing bracket
blocks slide on from the right: system prompt, user message, assistant reply
the eye at the centre watches everything on the belt
a fourth block arrives and the belt is full
the oldest block tips off the left edge and falls away

beats.narration_text: But the window isn't measured in words — it's measured in tokens. Tokenizers break text into subword pieces. The word “understanding” might be one token, but “tokenization” becomes three. On average, one token is about three-quarters of a word. So a 128K token window holds roughly 96,000 words — not 128,000.

show.event: 'understanding' lands under a single bracket — 1 token
'tokenization' splits into token · iz · ation, three brackets
the arithmetic resolves: 128,000 × 0.75 ≈ 96,000 words
two bars: 128K 'what people assume' above a visibly shorter 96K
the gap between them is called out

beats.narration_text: Here's the engineering problem. Attention — the mechanism that lets the model relate every token to every other token — scales quadratically. Double the context length, quadruple the computation. The KV cache stores the key and value vectors for tokens already processed, so the model doesn't recompute them on every new token. But that cache lives in GPU memory. A 128K window on a large model can consume tens of gigabytes of VRAM just for the cache.

show.event: a 1K × 1K attention grid appears
the length doubles to 2K and the grid's AREA quadruples
the grid compresses into two stacked blocks: K cache, V cache
a VRAM meter appears beside them
the context slider runs up to 128K and the meter fills
the label lands: ~40 GB, KV cache alone

beats.narration_text: And here's the real catch: a 128K-token window doesn't mean 128K tokens of equal attention. Research shows LLMs attend strongly to the beginning and end of the context, but struggle with information buried in the middle. It's called the “lost in the middle” effect. The window is technically open, but recall degrades. Position matters as much as presence.

show.event: the full window draws as one long bar
it shades by attention: bright at both ends, dim through the middle
the U-shaped curve resolves above it
a drops into the middle looking for a fact
it comes up empty — a '?' floats above it
the label lands: lost in the middle

props.sparkLine: Open is not the same as recalled.

beats.narration_text: So how do you work within these limits? Three strategies. Chunking: break long documents into pieces that fit. Summarization: compress prior conversation into a shorter recap. And RAG — retrieval-augmented generation — where you search a knowledge base and inject only the relevant pieces into the window. The context window is a budget. Spend it on what matters.

show.event: left: a long document splits into chunks that fit
centre: a tall conversation stack compresses into one recap block
right: a query hits a store and two relevant snippets fly out
the belt returns beneath all three
chunks, recap and snippets land on it, all inside the bracket
the closing line resolves: a budget — spend it on what matters

props.sparkLine: A budget. Spend it on what matters.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The window is a buffer measured in tokens, so the advertised number is about a quarter larger than the words you actually get. Holding it open is not free — attention cost grows with the square of the length, and the cache that avoids recomputing it is paid for in gigabytes of GPU memory. And a window being open is not the same as the model recalling what is in it: the middle is where things get lost. Treat it as a budget.

show.event: 0.5s lead pause, then ClaudeVerdictArtifact card builds in
line 1: tokens, not words
line 2: quadratic cost and the VRAM bill
line 3: recall is not uniform
line 4: the three workarounds

props.artifactTitle: what a context window really is
artifactLines: The window is a fixed buffer measured in tokens — roughly 0.75 words each.
Attention scales quadratically with length; the KV cache trades recomputation for VRAM, and at long contexts that bill is tens of gigabytes.
Recall is not uniform — the beginning and end are attended to far more strongly than the middle.
Chunking, summarization and retrieval all exist to spend a fixed budget on what matters.

beats.narration_text: That's the short version. The full video ends with a prompt you can run on your own longest prompt, to work out what in it is actually earning its place. Watch What a Context Window Really Is.

show.event: ClaudeTitleOutro: title in serif, terracotta period
subline fades in: 'a budget, not a memory'
